label: Concrete protocol version — Specific NMC811 pouch-cell target
question: Propose an evidence-supported starting fast-charge protocol for a 5 Ah graphite/NMC811 pouch cell at 25 °C, charging from 10% to 80% SOC with a target time of 20 minutes while limiting lithium plating. Give current stages and transition criteria only when supported, and clearly identify values that cannot be determined from the evidence.

conditions.objective: target 20 minutes while limiting lithium plating

what_it_tests: Concrete protocol version: whether detailed target conditions produce an ordered, experimentally actionable candidate protocol while clearly distinguishing reported, extrapolated, and unresolved values.

answer.summary: The evidence base is only partially matched to the requested graphite/NMC811, 5 Ah pouch cell at 25 °C. The strongest directly relevant findings are: (1) fast-charge protocols for graphite/NMC cells should reduce current as voltage rises to limit lithium plating; (2) for a modeled graphite/NMC532 cell, a 5C+CC stage should be terminated below 4.1 V to avoid plating, and multi-stage CC can reduce plating driving force relative to CCCV at very high initial rates; (3) a validated experimental fast-charge protocol on a constrained pouch cell at 25 °C achieved 0–85% SOC in 26.8 min with no abnormal capacity loss over 100 cycles, but the chemistry is not specified as NMC811 and the exact current steps are not in the retrieved chunk. Because no exact-match NMC811/5 Ah/25 °C/10–80%/20 min protocol was found, the suggestions below are conservative starting points synthesized or extrapolated from these sources and should be experimentally validated with cell-specific voltage, temperature, and plating diagnostics.

protocol_suggestions.rationale: This protocol is a conservative synthesis of the retrieved evidence. The model study reports that higher current should be used when voltage is low and lower current when voltage is high to avoid lithium plating, and that multi-stage CC can reduce plating driving force compared with CCCV at very high initial rates. The same study also indicates that for a graphite/NMC532 cell, a 5C+CC stage should be terminated below 4.1 V to prevent plating. The experimental constrained-pouch-cell study at 25 °C shows that a fast-charge protocol can reach 85% SOC in 26.8 min without abnormal capacity loss over 100 cycles, supporting the feasibility of a fast-charge starting point at this temperature, though the exact current profile is not available in the retrieved chunk. Because the requested chemistry is NMC811 rather than NMC532 and the cell is 5 Ah rather than the smaller modeled cell, the current values here are provisional starting values rather than directly reported settings.

This makes a conservative CC-to-CV profile a reasonable comparator for experimental screening, especially if the goal is to benchmark against a simpler protocol. The voltage cutoff should be conservative because the model study warns that a 5C+CC stage should end below 4.1 V to prevent plating in a graphite/NMC532 cell. However, because the evidence also suggests that multi-stage CC may be better than CCCV at extreme rates, this protocol should be treated as a baseline rather than the preferred final design.

Conclusions
Based on the features of the semi-optimal protocol, two practical novel fast charging protocols were proposed, namely the voltage ramping protocol and the multiple CCCV protocol. The simulation results showed that for the 2.5 mAh cm -2 cell, the maximum capacity after 10 min charge at 30 °C without lithium plating can be improved by up to 10.7% using the proposed protocols compared with the standard CCCV protocol. To achieve 80% charge in 10 min, the proposed protocols will require a charging temperature that is 8 °C lower than that of the CCCV protocol, which minimizes parasitic reactions and prolongs battery life. Finally, we predicted that the proposed protocols are more effective for the fast charging of high loading cells. For a 4 mAh cm -2 cell, the proposed protocols can improve the charge rate by up to 18.8% without lithium plating according to model prediction.
While this work only considered the driving force for lithium plating of a fresh cell as the optimization metric, other degradation mechanisms such as loss of lithium inventory, loss of active materials and increase of cell resistance can be taken into account in a similar manner. Also, these degradation mechanisms may change the lithium plating behavior of the cell, which necessitates adjusting the fast charge protocol as the cell ages. These will be the topics of our future work. Finally, results reported in this article are based on simulation only. Experimental validation of the proposed fast charging protocols is ongoing to verify their improved extreme fast charging capability and cycle life over traditional protocols.

Experimental
Table I lists the material, electrode, cell design parameters, and Table II includes the charging protocols. Graphite (1506T Superior Graphite) and NMC532 (Toda America) were used as respective negative and positive electrode active materials, respectively, to fabricate electrodes at the Cell Analysis, Modeling, and Prototyping (CAMP) Facility at Argonne National Laboratory (Argonne). These electrodes were cut and assembled in single layer pouch cells with Celgard 2320 separator. 1.2 M LiPF6 in a 3:7 by wt. ethylene carbonate: ethylmethyl carbonate electrolyte was used. The reversible capacity of the negative electrode and positive electrode at C/10 were measured to be 1.93 mAh cm -2 and 1.65 mAh cm -2 using half cells. The reversible negative to positive capacity ratio (N: P ratio) was set at 1.17 for C/10 rate (1.26 for C/1) by adjusting the mass loading of the electrodes for the operating cell voltage window of 3-4.1V. The cells were built such that the footprint of the negative electrode overhung the edge of the positive electrode by 0.5 mm on all sides. Such oversize accommodates slight imperfections of electrode alignment during cell assembly and avoid preferential plating of Li at the edges by guaranteeing there is Gr material directly opposite of the cathode.

Conclusions
In this work, the Pseudo2D electrochemical battery model was used to screen traditional fast charging protocols for a moderate HEV loading (2.5 mAh cm -2 ) graphite/NMC 532 cell. The simulation results showed that in terms of the maximum driving force for lithium plating, CCCV and CPCV protocols outperform the multistage constant-current charging with a single voltage cutoff and the pulse charging. To prevent lithium plating, the 5C + constant-current charging stage should be terminated at a voltage lower than 4.1 V for the investigated 2.5 mAh cm -2 cell. A fast charging algorithm was developed that charges the cell at close-to-maximum current at all time without causing lithium plating. The resultant semi-optimal protocol further illustrated that to achieve fast charging without lithium plating, the cell should be charged at a higher current when the cell voltage is low, and charged to higher voltage when the charge current is low.

Screening of Conventional Protocols Using the Pseudo2D Model
To investigate how the charge rate in fl uences the driving force of lithium plating, a parameter sweep is performed such that the investigated cell is charged with a wide range of n C CCCV and n P CPCV protocols, up to 10C and 10P, respectively. Figure 3 summarizes the simulation results, the x axis of which is the state-ofcharge (SOC = ò I t d /(35.25 mAh)) of the cell after 10 min charging while the y axis is the maximum driving force for lithium plating during the charging process, i.e., min( f f -s e ). The colorbar of the Fig. represents the mean cell temperature in 10 min. For both CCCV and CPCV charging, it can be seen from the Fig. that there is a strong correlation between charge rate, driving force for lithium plating, and mean cell temperature. To charge the cell to a higher SOC in 10 min, the cell has to be charged at higher C rate or higher power, which will lead to higher driving force for lithium plating and a higher mean cell temperature. For example, the cell can be charged to SOC = 73% in 10 min using the 10C CCCV protocol but with a high driving force for lithium plating (min f f -= -38 mV s e ( ) ) and a high mean cell temperature ( ∼ 34.5 °C). Results and Discussion
The shown fast charge protocol allows a charging of the cell from 0%SoC to 85%SoC in 26.8 min. To validate the developed charging protocol three cells were cycled with this protocol. Start condition was 25 °C ±1 °C cell temperature and the temperature of the chamber held constant. Cells were cycled in the already presented test setup (refer to Fig. 1) to realize the same test conditions as in second test case. The cycling was started at 0%SoC and the cell was charged with the optimized protocol. Afterwards for relaxation a waiting time of 1 h with following discharge with 1/3 C to 0%SoC has been done. Followed by a further relaxation phase of 2 h. This procedure was repeated for 100 cycles with a capacity check every 25 cycles. After these 100 cycles the state of health (short SoH) of tested cells compared to initial capacity was over 95% and no abnormalities (for example voltage shoulder during relaxation phase) during whole test time occurred. In comparison cycling the cells with same test procedure from 0% to 80% SoC with a constant charging current of 1/3 C at 25 °C for 100 cycles, show a discharge capacity loss of not even 4%, means a SoH of over 96%. During this test about 95% of the Ah throughput for the 100 cycles in comparison to 100 fast charge cycles has been done. Based on the comparison of capacity retention after 100cycles from both tests no abnormal capacity loss based on fast charging could be shown.

Screening of Conventional Protocols Using the Pseudo2D Model
As a result, at given min( f f -s e ) (determined by C rate in the fi rst stage), the cell SOC after 10 min charge with the multi-stage constant-current protocol is smaller than those with CCCV and CPCV, independent of how many CC steps are used as long as the cutoff voltage is fi xed at 4.1 V.
Note that a few data points of the multi-stage protocol show lower driving force of lithium plating than CCCV, when the charge acceptance in 10 min is higher than SOC = 72%. This is because to achieve such high charge acceptance in 10 min, the initial C rate of the CCCV protocol has to be suf fi ciently high ( ⩾ 8C). Due to the high initial C rate, the f f -s e continues to decrease during the CV charging of the CCCV protocol, resulting in a lower min f f -s e ( ) of the the CCCV protocol than the multi-stage constant-current protocol. Therefore, in such extreme high-rate charging the adoption of the multi-stage constant-current protocol is bene fi cial in terms of reducing the maximum driving force of lithium plating compared to CCCV/CPCV. However, it should be noted that multi-stage constant-current protocol still results in a high plating driving force in this case.

4. Applying the fast charging algorithm to a commercial lithium-ion battery: experimental validation
The test results obtained by applying the fast charging algorithm to a large-format commercial lithium-ion battery with an incorporated reference electrode are presented in this section. The commercial pouch cells consisted of NCM/graphite electrodes. The nominal capacity was 40 A h, and the voltage range was 2.84.2 V. To construct a three-electrode cell, the oxidation was removed from a 25l m-diameter copper wire by acid washing, and the wire was then placed on the surface of the anode/separator interface. The copper wire was wrapped with insulating tape to avoid short circuit. After the fresh was subjected to SEI formation cycles, lithium was electroplated onto the copper wire using a constant deposition current. To form a uniform lithium layer, the deposition current (50 l A for 1 h), was first applied between the copper wire and positive electrode and then between the copper wire and the negative electrode. Subsequently, the threeelectrode cells were subjected to a performance test followed by a series of fast charging experiments. An Arbin Battery Testing Instrument BT-5HC was utilized to charge and discharge the cells, and a temperature chamber was used to maintain a constant temperature during the tests. The schematic of the fast charging test platform is shown in Fig. 6. To meet the time-variable current requirement of the proposed algorithms, the software platform was specially designed for real-time signal processing and transmission.

Experimental
After each CC-charge test and following discharge a capacity check has been performed. In this check the cell was fully charged with 1/3 C followed by a constant voltage (short: CV) phase and after a suf fi cient relaxation time also discharged with 1/3 C to 0%SoC without CV phase. For all tested conditions in the test case two, new cells were used to eliminate the in fl uence of cell ageing due to lithium plating condition in the test before.
Figure 1. Test setup layout for constrained li-ion cell measurement.
The third investigated test case was an optimized fast charging protocol developed from the results of test case two. For testing the developed fast charging pro fi le, three new cells were cycled at a constant temperature in the chamber. Cycling means the cells were charged with the fast charging protocol and discharged with standard 1/3 C discharge rate to exclude additional cell ageing due to discharge conditions. Between charging and discharging as well as discharging and charging a relaxation phase of one hour was implemented.
